title: Live: Bombers unveil McVeigh as icon calls for unity after Hird snub
text:
Essendon legend Tim Watson has urged passionate Bombers fans to "put [their] weapons down" as the club gets ready to unveil Mark McVeigh as its new coach.

McVeigh was confirmed as the coach on Monday night, beating out fan favourite James Hird as well as Fremantle assistant Jaymie Graham and Adelaide's coaching director, Murray Davis.

The 45-year-old will be flanked by Essendon president Andrew Welsh and CEO Tim Roberts when he fronts the media from 11am AEST.

Live Moment Essendon president Andrew Welsh and CEO Tim Roberts unveil Mark McVeigh as the club's senior coach from 11am AEST. Welsh keen to have Hird involved at Essendon Welsh, like McVeigh, says he wants to see Hird back within the four walls. "I'd love to see James as a part of the club going forward. He's such a fantastic football person. "I feel there's significant value James can bring, not just tokenistic, but real value to our club and our playing group. "Certainly, part of my messaging was that Mark and I would want to catch up with him when the time is appropriate." Welsh says calls to Hird went unanswered Welsh says he tried to call Hird twice once the board had ratified McVeigh as the choice, but the phone went unanswered. He expects to talk to Hird today. Welsh on the 'Essendon person' rumours For a long time, people thought McVeigh and Hird having Essendon connections would make the coaching race a sham. Welsh disagrees. "Understanding the Essendon Football Club or being an Essendon person was something that wasn't held in as high a regard internally with the panel, that it was externally with some of the commentary going around." Welsh won't answer specifics on other candidates Welsh gets asked about questions he asked the other candidates, but refuses to entertain them. He says they all had different ideas on game plans. McVeigh 'absolutely' wants Solomon to stick around McVeigh downplays rumours of a feud with Solomon, and says he wants him to stick around next year. "We had one of the best embraces as mates today. "We've been mates since we were 15 years of age. We're absolutely fine, he's one of my best friends." McVeigh speaks on first meeting with Merrett One of McVeigh's first jobs will be deciding what happens with Zach Merrett. Here's what he said on his meeting with the ex-skipper. "Zach and I have just met earlier. I've got a huge amount of respect for Zach. "He's done so much for the club, you must respect your champions, I'm big on that. "I think it's really important we understand the players' feelings, it's not just about the club's feelings. "I want him to be here, but I'll listen to him as well." McVeigh to sound out potential assistants in coming days McVeigh says he has "a list of assistants" he wants to talk to. He will have those conversations in the coming days. McVeigh says he sought out Swans after GWS rejection McVeigh says he felt "comfortable and confident" that he could do the Bombers job if he'd won it. He said he sought out a role with Sydney after falling short in his bid to be GWS coach after Leon Cameron was let go. McVeigh says he will reach out to Hird on potential role "Going forward, I'll have those discussions with James, absolutely," he says. "I need to know where his footy journey is going to go from here." McVeigh says he spoke to Hird this morning Predictably, one of the first questions asked of McVeigh is about Hird. "I love James Hird, he's one of my best mates. It was difficult to go through the process against a good friend. "I don't fear those people [Hird's supporters], I actually embrace how they feel, and I understand it, to be fair. "He's been a constant in my life since I was 17 years of age. We spoke this morning, and the way he spoke of how proud he was of this moment for me, it hasn't broken us, we're still together, but I understand and embrace the feelings of the people that love James Hird, because I do too." Show more

Watson, who is arguably the most prominent Essendon voice in the media, said McVeigh's appointment presented an opportunity for unity.

"There's got to be a unification of the club now," he told SEN on Tuesday morning.

"People have to put down their weapons and get behind this appointment of a former player — somebody who has been passionate about the football club.

"This is part of the healing process that needs to take place. Ultimately, it's a much bigger thing than the emotion that might be associated with it now. There is an enormous amount of work to do.

Tim Watson (pictured) has called for unity at Essendon after Mark McVeigh's signing. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

"Congratulations to him. He's been an Essendon man all his life. He's loved this football club, that was clear in the days that he played.

"He's had a great development profile if you look at where he's been and what he's been doing. He's been part of elite coaching departments [at GWS and Sydney]."

Despite beating Hird out for the role, McVeigh shares a strong relationship with his former captain.

McVeigh was prepared to be an assistant under Hird when Hird previously attempted to return as Essendon coach at the end of 2022, before the club appointed Brad Scott instead.

Fellow Essendon great Matthew Lloyd, who also has a relationship with McVeigh, lauded his appointment, indicating McVeigh would be happy to work with Hird.

"All I will say is, Mark would love to have James Hird as part of his staff," Lloyd told Nine's Footy Classified on Monday night.

"He [Hird] may say, 'You are kidding, there's no way I'm coming, after being overlooked', but Mark would certainly be open to it."

McVeigh has signed a three-year contract with Essendon and was the unanimous choice of the Essendon board.

title: Wiring issue causes second Sydney train delay in a fortnight
text:
Some Sydney commuters are facing long lines for replacement buses after overhead wiring issues caused train delays for the second time in almost as many weeks.

The city-bound service between Gordon and Chatswood on the T1 North Shore Line has been replaced with buses on Tuesday morning.

Sydney Trains said the wiring failed overnight, and services on the T1 line and the T9 Northern Line had been hardest hit.

"We had what's called a loss of tension in the overhead wire at Chatswood, so the line that powers the train, due to a failure in one of the counterweights," Sydney Trains CEO Matthew Longland said.

"So we have very heavy weights that hang off to the side that keep the tension, keep the wires held up. One of those counterweights failed last night.

"The counterweights are inspected regularly, so we'll obviously look at the history of this particular location, whether there was any incident there that was a problem."

Replacement buses have been made available to morning commuters facing train delays. (ABC News)

Mr Longland said crews had been working through the night to fix the issue.

He told 702 ABC Sydney about 8:30am that primary repairs were "now complete".

"There's still a little bit of secondary work to do before the power gets turned on, but we're targeting later this morning to have the repairs complete, have the lines re-energised, and have trains operating back on the T1 line as normal towards the city," he said.

Aerial vision shows a train stopped on the tracks at Artarmon on Sydney's lower north shore. (ABC News)

Passengers have been urged to allow extra travel time.

"We've got extra staff on the ground to assist passengers and the peak has flowed well," Mr Longland said.

"Heading towards the city from Chatswood, obviously Sydney Metro would be the best way to get to the city for people that need to connect into town."

"For those passengers up at the Hornsby end, we are operating a normal service on the T9 line that runs via Strathfield into the city."

Second incident in 11 days

A crowd gathered at Chatswood Station. (ABC News: Monish Nand)

Commuters told the ABC they had been "packed like sardines", saying the metro could not handle the amount of customers now going on that service.

"I usually just go to Gordon, just to get to uni, because I go from Gordon and Chatswood, but I had to travel all the way from Chatswood instead. Now I'm late," one woman said.

" The trains are super unreliable. I've been in situations where I've had no way to get home before. "

The incident comes less than two weeks after a "freak issue" caused major delays to afternoon services on Friday, August 14.

Hundreds of people had to be assisted off trains after overhead wires came down onto a train.

At the time, Transport for NSW secretary Josh Murray said "every centimetre of overhead wiring" had been scanned as part of a $2.1 billion uplift of the network.

Crews had been working throughout the night to address the issue this week. (ABC News)

Some bus marshals have been deployed at key stations to help passengers on Tuesday.

"For locals that are travelling into the city, they might be able to also catch a normal scheduled bus service," Mr Longland said.

"Check on the Opal app because that might be a quicker way rather than lining up for a bus at a train station."

Changes have been made to the T1 Western Line with some services from Penrith, Emu Plains and Richmond which usually go to Lindfield and Gordon terminating at North Sydney to "reduce some of the congestion on the line where we're doing the work".

The Central Coast line has also been impacted, with all trains to the city operating via Strathfield.

title: Piastri searching for answers as teammate re-enters F1 title picture
text:
Oscar Piastri's "disappointing" end to the Dutch Grand Prix has left the Australian and his McLaren team searching for answers, while his teammate has roared back into the Formula 1 title picture.

Last weekend in Zandvoort was shaping to be a good weekend for Piastri.

The Australian was matching the pace at the front through qualifying, and after a terrific second start in the grand prix following Max Verstappen's heavy crash, Piastri was on course for a first podium finish since Miami in May.

Piastri struggles after slow pit stop, Norris wins as Verstappen crashes Reigning world champion Lando Norris has doubled his grand prix win tally in 2026, producing a pair of brilliant overtakes to win the Dutch Grand Prix.

Piastri had performed a breathtaking overtake on Mercedes driver George Russell to move into third and was not far off the pace set by leaders Kimi Antonelli and teammate Lando Norris, despite being on a harder compound tyre.

But a slow first pit stop knocked Piastri back behind Russell and out of third place, and it only got worse from there.

Piastri, who won the Dutch Grand Prix in 2025, fell right off the pace and finished a distant sixth as Norris surged to victory.

Piastri was running third until a slow pit stop knocked him out of the podium position at Zandvoort. (Reuters: Benoit Tessier)

The sudden pace drop-off has left Piastri with plenty of questions that he and the team will want answers to.

"The first stint felt reasonable, but from the second stint onwards, the pace was simply not there, and it became a real struggle," he said.

"We will review the entire weekend and analyse to understand why we experienced such a significant performance drop-off.

"A slow pit stop didn't help, but the fundamental issue was the lack of pace, which is something we'll work on ahead of Monza.

"That's the priority now, to dig into the data with the team to find the root cause and ensure we can move forward in a more positive direction for the upcoming races."

Piastri's situation is a far cry from where he was at the conclusion of last year's Dutch Grand Prix, when he claimed his seventh grand prix win of the season and was the championship leader.

But while Piastri is seeking answers to get back to the front of the grid, Norris is threatening to stay there.

'The fight's still on': Norris re-enters the F1 title picture

McLaren entered the 2026 season having won the previous two constructors' championships, and with Lando Norris as reigning drivers' champion.

Reigning Formula 1 drivers' champion Lando Norris has won the past two grands prix. (Reuters: Benoit Tessier)

But with a new era of regulations, McLaren's 2026 season started poorly.

Piastri crashed on his way to the grid in Melbourne and he and Norris did not start in Shanghai due to car issues.

Norris then had back-to-back retirements in Montreal and Monaco, meaning he failed to finish three of the opening six grands prix.

But the reigning world champion has returned to winning ways, triumphing in Hungary before the mid-year break and then again last weekend in the Netherlands.

With back-to-back wins and growing confidence in his season, Norris has re-emerged as a drivers' championship contender.

F1 drivers' championship standings after Dutch Grand Prix 242 — Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes

183 — George Russell, Mercedes

183 — Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari

159 — Lando Norris, McLaren

155 — Charles Leclerc, Ferrari

With 10 or 11 rounds remaining this season, depending on conflict in the Middle East, Norris is sitting fourth in the standings, 83 points behind leader Kimi Antonelli.

It is a huge gap, but recent history shows it is not an impossible feat.

At the conclusion of last year's Dutch Grand Prix, Max Verstappen was 104 points behind then-leader Piastri with nine rounds remaining.

Verstappen surged towards the end of the season while Piastri slumped. Verstappen fell two points shy of Norris in the standings, but finished a stunning 11 points ahead of Piastri.

Having seen what is possible, Norris has made this year's title fight a four-way race with Antonelli, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton.

Norris's message to his team over the radio after taking the chequered flag on Sunday certainly sounded like the Briton believed his championship hopes are far from over.

"Let's keep pushing. Thank you for the hard work. Let's keep bringing upgrades, let's keep bringing performance, please," he said.

"The fight's still on."

Out of the car, Norris was quick to point out that there is a long season still ahead of the drivers and that he was not getting ahead of himself with an 83-point deficit.

"One race at a time. A lot of people say it now, but it is the truth of it. There's no point in thinking that far ahead," he said after winning on Sunday.

"There are plenty of things we can do better, and we need to do better if we want to fight for a championship.

"We have to keep working hard. There's still plenty of races, plenty of opportunity for everyone."

Norris's deficit to Antonelli was 101 points prior to the weekend in Hungary, but the McLaren champion has reduced that by 18 with two tremendous weekends.

However, the 83-point gap is significant and Antonelli has extended his overall championship lead.

Entering the Dutch Grand Prix weekend, the young Italian's lead over Hamilton was 50 points, and 59 over Russell.

After the weekend, his lead is 59 points over both Hamilton and Russell.

F1 heads to Monza for the Italian Grand Prix in two weeks, one of the fastest tracks on the calendar and vastly different to the tight and twisting circuits in Hungary and the Netherlands where Norris has won this year.

title: Two ABC presenters share stories of 35 years in media
text:
In a cutthroat and ever-changing industry, 102.5 ABC Perth's Mark Gibson and Nadia Mitsopoulos have each reached a significant milestone — working in the media industry for 35 years.

This is how it all began.

Nadia Mitsopoulos: I always wanted to be a journalist in high school. I remember very vividly watching TV news one night with my father. Brian Burke was on the TV, who was our then premier. And I said to my dad, "Oh, what were his qualifications to become a premier?" And he said he was a journalist and actually a very good one. And that's where I thought, "Ah, OK, yeah, that's the job that sort of fits in with what I want to do".

Mark Gibson: I vividly remember also watching the news with my dad because in our house, the TV wasn't allowed to go on until the evening news. And Dad was glued to the commercial news, then the ABC news, then the 7.30 report. And we just watched news.

Nadia Mitsopoulos in the Great Southern, where she worked for GWN from 1991 to 1993. (Supplied: Nadia Mitsopoulos)

Nadia: I went to Curtin University. I was there for three years doing a journalism major. In my third year, halfway through, GWN were calling out for cadets. I applied for one, didn't get it. The person that did get it left three months later. I rang the news director back and said, "Hey, how about it?" And then I called him every day for eight days until he offered me the job. I think he was just sick of my phone calls. He gave me a week to get down to Bunbury. And that's where it started.

Mark: I was always good at English, loved to write, so thought I would be a print journalist and started the same Curtin journalism degree. I was only in my first year when I learned about a WAAPA (Western Australian Academy of Performing Arts) broadcasting course. I auditioned and I got in. They only accepted 18 people. In August of the second year, I specifically remember it being pinned on our notice board at WAAPA, there was a job going for a radio announcer at Northwest Radio in Karratha.

The salary was $17,000 a year. I got the job and I left in the August. I didn't finish the course so I have no tertiary qualifications. The advice I got at the time was just go for the job. The job is better than any piece of paper.

Mark Gibson at Northwest Radio in 1991. (Supplied: Mark Gibson)

Nadia: Gibbo, I was making $1,000 more than you with my first job, $18,000. I thought it was absolutely the best. I did Bunbury and then got moved to Albany and had an absolute ball.

With regional postings, you do everything. You're the political reporter, the council reporter, the sports reporter, the environment reporter. You name it, you do it all. It's a really good way to learn how to establish contacts in a town. Also, appreciating the sensitivities of a town when there are horrible stories. And I've got to say, in Albany we had plenty of them.

Mark: Nadia launched straight into journalism. My job was more the radio announcing and playing music and DJing at the local pub to start off with before I really moved into the news path.

I left Karratha after nine months and I didn't even have enough money for an airfare home. My parents said, "No worries, we'll meet you at the bus station." And I caught the bus back from Karratha, 24 hours on a bus. I had about $2 to my name, moved back in at home with Mum and Dad. I was 20 years old and thankfully within a few weeks, I got a job in a radio newsroom in Perth and started again.

Nadia (second from right) with colleagues at Channel 10 at the office in Dianella, where she worked from 1993 to 1996. (Supplied: Nadia Mitsopoulos)

After their country stints, Nadia moved to Perth to work in commercial television news, eventually specialising in state politics, while Mark moved to Sydney, working at radio station 2GB, covering crime.

Mark: In Sydney in the 90s, I was covering murders, serial killers, I ended up covering the backpacker murders, the trial of Ivan Milat, some horrific things, I mean, we're talking Sydney. I remember covering the New South Wales police royal commission with the most horrible stories of police corruption and the protection of paedophiles, you name it. This was eye-opening stuff for someone in their 20s from Perth.

In the 90s, journalists operated without the internet or mobile phones.

Mark: I still have no idea how we did it. I just remember picking up landlines. In radio days, pulling over on the side of the road and filing a story from a public phone box, that's how you would do it. And then those early days of reporting in Sydney was around the time we were getting the huge mobile phones. I remember going out to law courts with a bag over my shoulder that contained a huge phone. I would then be able to step out of the court and file a story. I thought that was so fancy.

Nadia: We would call the office on a public phone box; we could reverse charges in the country areas. We had the telex machine and that would spit out the weather. The electoral roll would be on microfiche, and we'd have to put it under the little telescope to find John Smith, who lives in Karrinyup, but I'd have to ring 28 John Smiths to get to the one I wanted. It was laborious work.

Mark Gibson reporting on the Bali bombings in 2002. (Supplied: Mark Gibson)

Mark: And the old-fashioned contact book. I found my original contact book not long ago and I had a home phone number for Carmen Lawrence, who was the premier at the time. It was the only way to get people.

Nadia: Everyone picked up the phone back then. We didn't have call screening, so you didn't know who was ringing you. The phone would ring; you'd pick it up.

Sometimes, people would just smack the phone down. The other thing you would do was rock up at their door, and that would happen a lot.

We had time to investigate stories, find the right people to talk to. We only had to worry about the 6 o'clock bulletin; back then we didn't have to worry about multiple platforms.

Nadia Mitsopoulos at her desk at Channel 10 in 1997. (Supplied: Nadia Mitsopoulos)

Mark: Now, it's get the story and get it out on every platform quickly. That's changed a lot, but you've also got the benefits of technology. Now you can report live on TV from anywhere at any time. In the old days, you had to set up a satellite truck and it would take forever and you just couldn't do it. These days, it's all just so immediate.

Nadia: I spent 13 years up at parliament and when a report was tabled, and this is in the early 2000s, I had time to read the report because I had time between that report being tabled at 12 o'clock and my 6 o'clock bulletin to actually go through it and get the good stuff, not just the two-page executive summary at the front. You had more investigative capabilities back then because you had more time, but the newsrooms were bigger, there was more staff.

What have been some of the highlights of your careers?

Mark Gibson: For me, it all culminated with the Sydney Olympics in 2000. I was the chief Olympics reporter for Channel 10 and covered every single minute of the Olympics. That was just incredible. We got housed out near Homebush for three weeks. I travelled around the world; went to Greece for the lighting of the Olympic flame; went to Uluru for the Olympic flame arriving in Australia; travelled around the torch relay; ended up in Sydney. It was just the most amazing event to cover. And it all was so positive, so happy. Then not long after returning to Perth in 2001, there was 9/11 and the following year I was sent straight up to Bali for the Bali bombings, which was the most challenging assignment I've ever covered in my life.

Mark Gibson at the athletics at the Sydney Olympics in 2000. (Supplied: Mark Gibson)

Nadia: I love my politics. Laurie Connell being released from jail. And we were out there from 4am and it was pouring with rain. But of course, he just gets released at 9 o'clock like every other prisoner does and there was the big media pack. I managed to get on my hands and knees and crawl into the pack and I went, "Excuse me, Mr Connell, excuse me," he looked down and I said, "What's the one thing you're looking forward to?" And he said: "A big plate of seafood."

I also witnessed Brian Burke being released from jail. They were huge stories. I used to bother Brian Burke quite a bit and he once told me I am like death and taxes — I'll never go away. I took that as a compliment.

At WA parliament house for Channel 9 with journalist colleagues. (Supplied: Nadia Mitsopoulos)

On coming to radio after decades in television, Nadia joined 102.5 ABC Perth in 2012 as a producer, moving into presenting in 2018, while Mark came on board to present the breakfast program in 2024.

Mark: It's full circle for me, which is great. I had 25 years in TV. To come back to radio where I started is so much fun because it's just a whole different way of storytelling and communicating directly with people. It's really rewarding.

Nadia: I went straight into TV, which was kind of rare. I'd always liked radio. I did some segments with Geoff Hutchison when he was doing the morning show. Then I actually just got to a point where I think the TV industry was changing and I wasn't changing with it. An opportunity came up when my kids were young to work part-time with Geoff Hutchison. So I took it.

I loved the immediacy of it. I've always loved the chase of a story and as a producer, you can do that when there'd be some big breaking story. And I still had a damn good contact book.

Mark: Radio allows you to tell the story properly, unedited, unfiltered and giving people that platform is such a joy.

Nadia Mitsopoulos and Mark Gibson in the 102.5 ABC Perth studio. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

Do you think about what your next role in media might be?

Mark: I honestly don't think about it. I get up every morning, and I honestly say that I bounce into work and love what I do. And that's all you can hope for. I don't really think now about anything that comes next. I just love the fact I get to do this every day.

Nadia: I do think about a conversation that I had with Russell Woolf, about two weeks before he died and he said, "I think this will be the job I will have until I retire." And I did say to him, "I think I feel the same way." I don't know when that will be though because I'm in no rush.

Mark and Nadia are celebrating the milestone with an event at the new Edith Cowan University city campus on August 27, when listeners and media students will turn the microphone on them as they share the highs and lows of surviving (and thriving) for 35 years.

title: Live: Coles posts $1.1b annual profit, $235m set aside for worker underpayments
text:
Let's get into a bit more of Business Council of Australia's (BCA) chief executive Bran Black's speech, with a focus on some pretty radical honesty: how poorly the business community has made its case to the public in recent years.

"Too much of our nation's economic discourse occurs between governments, business groups, unions, economists and commentators," he says. "Meanwhile, Australians are trying to pay the mortgage or find somewhere affordable to rent. "And work out how they can possibly afford for their kids the same opportunities they had while growing up. "Put simply, we know that the often-referenced Betty from Blacktown doesn’t care about our rate of productivity, but we know she does care about her cost of living."

Here's what I think is the key bit:

"We talk about productivity, regulation and the importance of investment. All of that matters. But too often, we — collectively — fail to explain why it matters, and critically, why its absence or reduction affects people's lives day to day. That has to change, and to do it, we must do a better job making the case to all Australians. "If we want Australians to support the economic reform needed to become a top 10 investment destination, they need to be able to see and understand why it helps them and, conversely, why its absence hinders their prosperity."

The BCA's idea is to combine with around 30 other national organisations under the banner of the Alliance of Industry Associations.

"Together, we represent businesses large and small across almost every part of the Australian economy, from pharmacists to farmers, and from tradies to accountants. And we're united by a simple objective: to help build support for reforms that will allow all Australians to get ahead," Mr Black says.

"That means changing the way we have economic conversations. "It means teasing out the real drivers of cost pressures Australians are feeling. It means listening to workers, families, small businesses and communities. "And it means doing a better job connecting what’s happening in their lives with the economic choices we make as a country. "Simply put, business cannot ask government to be ambitious for Australia if we're not prepared to help build that support ourselves. And that's the work that the Alliance of Industry Associations will take forward."

A reminder that this speech has not yet been delivered, but will be this evening at a gala dinner.

title: Home owner blindsided by agents who allegedly secretly bought his home
text:
A Perth real estate agency that allegedly ran a "ghost" open home before using a shell company to purchase the property it had been hired to sell has been reprimanded by consumer authorities.

The home owner believes more should have been done, with the case prompting calls for stronger penalties to be applied for breaches of conflict-of-interest rules.

Home owner Chao "Jack" Wu believes he received almost $100,000 less than his house was worth when his property was sold in 2024 by Ideal Realty WA to the firm's own real estate agents.

The real estate agents — Roy Li, whose legal name is Liang Li, and Lynn Ding, who goes by Lynn Ting but whose legal name is Lin Ding — deny they failed to disclose that they were the real buyers before making an offer on the property.

They also dispute they paid less than it was worth.

Jack sells his first home

Jack purchased his first home in Western Australia in 2020, six years after settling in Perth from China.

He invested tens of thousands of dollars in the property, a brick and tile 1970s build in the eastern suburb of Kenwick, renovating the driveway and installing a granny flat out the back.

In 2024, Jack signed an exclusive sales agreement on April 23 with Ideal Realty WA, which advertises itself as a multi-award-winning boutique agency with more than a decade operating in Perth.

Mr Wu signed the offer contract for the sale of the house on April 29. (Supplied: Jack Wu)

Six days later, he received an email from Ms Ding, copying in Mr Li, saying they had received three offers for his home, the highest of which was from a company called Generation Two PTY LTD.

"The buyer is almost a cash offer, we recommend to accept the offer and get it secure, or the buyer will offer another property," the email said.

Mr Li also sent Mr Wu a few texts that day, telling him:

April 29, 2024 12:20pm Roy Li: "The buyer has no finance issue and we can accept it or the buyer will offer others after compared (sic)".

April 29, 2024 1:24pm Roy Li: "Will do the best to deal with the buyers. No worries".

April 29, 2024 1:24pm Roy Li: "Not easy to hold the buyers too long :)"

Jack said he signed a sale contract with Generation Two later that afternoon after making a counteroffer for an additional $20,000.

'Weird' feeling

But a few weeks later, he said he had a "weird" feeling after an adjustment had been made to the name of the buyer on the sale contract after it had already been countersigned by both parties.

Jack then decided to try to find out more details about Generation Two, and ordered corporate documents from the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC), which revealed the owners were Mr Li and Ms Ding.

The documents also showed Generation Two was established and registered at Ideal Realty WA's office address on the same day the offer was made on Jack's home.

On the sale contract, the company was listed as registered at a different, residential address, being Mr Li's postal address.

Jack received an offer to buy his home from a company named Generation Two, which corporate records show was owned by his real estate agents. (ABC News: Rebecca Trigger)

Jack said when he confronted them with these details, Mr Li and Ms Ding agreed to pay him another $10,000 and to also waive the agents' sale fee of $10,000.

He said that only then, almost six weeks after the initial sale contract was signed, did Mr Li send him a disclosure form to sign, acknowledging their interest in the purchase.

In WA, it is against the law for a real estate agent to be a party in a transaction for a property they have been hired to sell, unless they obtain prior written consent from the owner.

Jack said he went ahead with the sale because he believed, as he had already signed a sale contract, he would be liable for damages if he pulled out of the transaction.

Do you know more about this story? Contact Rebecca Trigger.

Agent denies not disclosing he was buyer

When the ABC asked Mr Li why he had referred to himself as "the buyer" in his texts and emails with Jack, he said he could not recall the specifics of these messages, but believed he would have communicated about himself in the third person because he was also the agent.

Mr Li also said he had told Jack before making the offer that he and Ms Ding were the buyers and had negotiated the purchase price directly with him.

"Before the settlement, before we are doing the finance, before everything, he knows we're the buyer," Mr Li said.

He did acknowledge, however, that Jack only signed the disclosure form weeks after the sale contract was signed.

He initially claimed Jack refused to sign the disclosure form as a way of negotiating a higher price for the property, something Jack denies.

"The timing of the written disclosure was an administrative oversight, and our procedures have since been reviewed to ensure this does not occur again," Mr Li said in a later statement to the ABC.

Mr Li says he listed a residential address alongside Generation Two on the sale contract, instead of its true registered address, which was the same as Ideal Realty's office address, because that was his postal address at the time.

'Ghost' open home prompts questions

Jack is unclear on what home inspections were conducted before Mr Li and Ms Ding made the offer on his home.

He alleges Ideal Realty held a "ghost" open home designed "to suppress my price expectations".

Mr Li sent Jack a text message the day before he presented the Generation Two purchase offer, saying 13 groups had joined an open home and two groups had been booked for private viewings.

Many potential buyers don't need to inspect the property themselves, Mr Li said. (ABC News: Graeme Powell)

Jack said he later spotted a Google review on Ideal Realty WA from a punter complaining that they had showed up to a scheduled home inspection at that address but were told it was cancelled.

The ABC spoke with that potential buyer, who confirmed when she arrived at the property that day the agent present told her that the home inspection had been cancelled.

In response to the allegation, Mr Li told the ABC the rental tenant had refused to allow access to the inside of the property, so potential buyers were only able to view the outside.

But he said he held private viewings at the property before presenting the offers.

He also said potential buyers had become more comfortable with making offers based on seeing videos and photos since the COVID pandemic.

"So many investors they don't need to see the property," Mr Li said.

"They just check up the floor area, … from the photos they can see the property condition."

Conflicting valuations

Last year, Jack obtained legal advice and had the property retrospectively valued at the point of sale.

He said it put the value of the property at $800,000, or $95,000 more than what Mr Li and Ms Ding paid.

The annual growth of house prices in Perth still sits at 22.7 per cent, though it has slightly softened in recent months. (ABC News: Kenith Png)

Mr Li also said he had the property retrospectively valued, which put its price at between $680,000 and $705,000.

He said he believed Jack was disappointed because shifts in the market meant the property was now worth more.

" He feels he lost money," Mr Li said. "But sorry man, that's your choice. You made a final decision. "

Consumer watchdog issues formal warning

Jack complained to Consumer Protection, which investigated his case and issued a formal warning to Ideal Realty relating to an alleged conflict of interest.

A formal warning is issued by the department when it believes there is a prima facie case of a contravention of consumer law.

It also found Ideal Realty allegedly breached sections of the real estate code of conduct dealing with the requirement for agents to act in the best interests of their clients, duty of care, duty for honesty and misleading or deceptive conduct.

The department issues warnings when it believes consumer law has been breached. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

Breaches can result in fines of $5,000 for individuals and $25,000 for companies, but Ideal Realty WA was not issued a fine.

Consumer Protection does not publish details of administrative warnings and said it could not comment directly on its investigation.

A spokesperson, however, said in general it was lawful for a real estate agent to buy a property from their client, however they must disclose the interest to the seller before any negotiations take place, so the seller can make an informed decision.

Real estate lawyer, academic and commentator Tim O'Dwyer said there was a clear risk of a conflict of interest when an agent wanted to buy their client's home.

He described the Consumer Protection warning as a "slap across the knuckles with a feather" and urged sellers not to agree to offers in these circumstances without seeking independent legal advice and an independent property valuation.

"A buyer wants to pay the lowest possible price, and an agent's duty is to get the highest possible price," Mr O'Dwyer said.

title: Housing service tells single mother of four children to pitch a tent
text:
Tiffany Emmerson and her four children started couch surfing in December 2025 after she separated from her partner.

The single mother said the looming threat of having to live out of her car filled her with fear.

The 33-year-old said she tried to protect her children from the reality of their situation but said they were confused by the instability.

"You can't really explain to a two-year-old, a four-year-old and a seven-year-old what's going on," Ms Emmerson said.

"They just have questions of, 'Why are we at this person's house? Why are we staying here? Why are we staying there?'"

Her youngest is six weeks old.

Tiffany Emmerson packs a bag for her children. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

'Dire' situation

Ms Emmerson said she had reached out to every homeless and housing service across Townsville but had been knocked back by each one.

She said one told her to "buy a tent and find somewhere to go and pitch it".

"There's just no houses available, there's just nothing. Apparently, there's no shelters for people to go to, there's no emergency accommodation," she said.

" There's absolutely nothing. People are living in tents. "

Ms Emmerson said RentConnect, a service helping people find private rental housing, told her they could not help her because she did not meet the financial threshold.

For now, she is staying with her aunt, Kristy Emmerson, who lives in public housing.

Kristy Emmerson tries to keep a sense of normalcy for the children, keeping them entertained with toys and puzzles. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

It is a temporary fix with no long-term solution and, if her aunt decided to move out of the property, Ms Emmerson and her children would have nowhere to go.

Kristy said she felt terrible about the situation and it was affecting her mental health.

"This is Australia. When was it ever OK for people to not have a home, a roof over their heads?" she said.

Although Tiffany has an approved application for public housing, she still does not know when or if a property will become available.

She said many others were in a vulnerable position similar to hers.

Every time Tiffany Emmerson moves to a different location, she has to repack all her belongings, including a steriliser and clean bottles for her bottle-fed newborn baby. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

'Huge gap' in Townsville

Townsville Housing and Homeless Network (HaHN) chair Kym Musumeci said, despite lobbying for a dedicated homeless shelter for more than two years, no progress had been made.

"We've taken it to Canberra, we've taken it to the [housing] department, we've taken it to any local member that will listen to us, basically anyone who will listen to us," she said.

She warned there was a huge number of people seeking support.

"We have families sleeping in cars, we have seen an increase in tents popping up around Townsville," she said.

Last Thursday, more than 1 tonne of "rubbish, abandoned belongings, and other waste" was cleared from three "unoccupied, illegal" camps across the city, according to Mayor Nick Dametto.

The photo was posted to social media by Mayor Nick Dametto. (Supplied)

Ms Musumeci said 50 to 80 people turned up to the Red Cross homeless hub each day, but it did not have the resources to support them.

Seeking somewhere safe to sleep

"If we've got a stable shelter where people can go to be safe and secure and access supports whenever they need them, it's going to go a long way," she said.

HaHN has launched a petition for a shelter.

In response, a spokesperson for Queensland Housing Minister Sam O'Connor thanked the community for their advocacy but did not clarify whether the government planned to establish a homeless shelter.

The spokesperson said in Townsville, the government had added 110 social and affordable homes since being elected, with construction on a further 349 homes underway.

In 2025–26, $32.6 million was allocated to fund 17 specialist homelessness services in Townsville, providing 175 places of temporary supported accommodation, alongside outreach and support services, according to the statement.

Statewide, there are more than 44,000 people on the public housing list.

In Townsville, there are 3,558, down from 4,023 last year.

Funding cuts

The opposition's housing spokesperson, Meaghan Scanlon, said the government had changed the rules around eligibility for crisis accommodation.

Meaghan Scanlon says the state government is actively cutting the supports that would help people who are struggling right now. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

"There's a number of people who are being exited from social housing, and so that's why Queensland is experiencing homelessness in our streets and in our parks," she said.

"It's so frustrating that the Crisafulli government have decided to cut $42 million of funding from crisis accommodation in just this year alone."

She said the government was trying to suggest everything was OK but said she had spoken to many single mothers and their kids who were sleeping in cars.

"It's just not acceptable that a mum and her kids are being told there's nothing the government can do to help," Ms Scanlon said.

" That is just not OK in a wealthy state like Queensland. "

Tiffany Emmerson says she has seen other mums posting on social media about their struggles to find housing. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

Tiffany Emmerson said it had all been an "absolute stressful nightmare".

"We need more emergency temporary housing that's safe and suitable for families until they can get back on their feet and find a place," she said.

title: The gallery helping neurodivergent artists bridge gaps in the art world
text:
Maya Tamang says she "ain't no fancy bird", but you wouldn't know if you met her.

At Melbourne CBD gallery Jump Left, which is hosting her first solo show, she is resplendent in a frilly pink dress, dinner jacket with zebra print detailing, a pink pompom scarf and a bedazzled pink headdress.

"My way of communicating at social events is through outrageous fashion and glamour because you kind of can skip small talk," she says.

Tamang has autism, which can make the highly social art world especially difficult to navigate.

"I ain't no fancy bird" is the name of her show, a celebration of all things glitz, glamour and camp.

Sim Luttin's Jump Left gallery works with artists with an experience of disability. (ABC News: Ethan Seiderman)

In one portrait on display, comedian and cabaret performer Reuben Kaye poses in an outrageous hat shaped like a pair of lips with "Hollywood" scrawled across in gold.

The world Tamang paints harks back to a more elaborate past, one she became fascinated with as a child.

References to old Hollywood films, Elizabeth Taylor and Liberace find their way onto her canvases, as well as custom-decorated boots and headwear.

"Ever since I was a young girl, I was quite close with my grandma," she says.

"She lived in a home that looked like it was from a different time, and she loved all those films too.

"They felt so distant and other-worldly to me that I almost wanted to be in those films."

Comedian and cabaret performer Reuben Kaye is one of Tamang's muses. (Supplied: Naomi Matthews )

Kaye, who took over as artistic director of the Adelaide Cabaret Festival this year, is exactly the kind of larger-than-life figure Tamang is drawn to. He sat for the portraits over several sessions.

"Sitting for anything is an odd experience," Kaye says.

"I'm a doing person, and being the subject for a painting is in many ways a passive role. But sitting for Maya was joyous and chaotic."

A number of portraits hanging throughout the gallery space show Kaye adorned in garish costumes.

"Maya has a unique, messy, chaotic eye that throws finesse and refinement out the window in favour of chaos, and almost a primal, messy expression of queerness that owes more to punk than some might expect," Kaye says.

Tamang came to art as a teenager, not through school — which she never finished — but through art therapy sessions subsidised by the NDIS.

Painting gave her a way to express things that were hard to put into words.

"Separating myself from what's going on around me and putting my head down and working is my escape," she says.

Maya Tamang's work makes references to old Hollywood films, among other themes. (Supplied: Helga Salwe)

A few years ago, a solo show in a CBD gallery would have seemed impossible. Tamang was in and out of the psychiatric unit at Broadmeadows Hospital, in the city's north.

"I felt really stuck for a long time," she says.

Tamang, whose father is Nepalese, didn't always feel like she fit in.

"Growing up, [I felt] a bit of shame and stigma about my background," she says.

"I just really wanted to do everything I could to just fit in and not be bullied and survive.

"But being an adult, coming back with fresh eyes, I'm proud of it."

'Artist's vision' central to gallery's approach

Art helped Tamang make it out of those tough times, but turning it into a career was the harder next step.

Hands On Studio turns 30 as artist hopes Gillard portrait hangs in parliament Artist Stephen Corsini has been attending Canberra's Hands On Studio for 30 years. Now, he hopes his portrait of Australia's first female prime minister will hang in Parliament House.

Every artist has to deal with the business around the work: the funding applications, the correspondence with galleries, the framing, the installation.

Tamang says for a neurodivergent artist, that side of things can be the most difficult part, and the point where a career can stall.

Jump Left, which started in 2024, exists to help artists through exactly this. Tamang found her way to the gallery, which works with artists who are neurodivergent or living with disability, less than a year ago through a mutual friend she met at an exhibition opening.

"There are small and large supported studios that have really big group settings for artists to connect," director Sim Luttin says.

"We're more one-on-one in the way we work with artists."

Maya Tamang at Jump Left gallery. (Supplied: Astrid Mulder)

What that one-on-one support looks like in practice is often small and practical. Take the artist statement, the short piece of writing that accompanies almost any show. Most artists write their own. Tamang, who finds writing hard, wrote hers with Luttin.

The statement for Tamang's solo show came out of a series of conversations. Luttin would record Tamang talking, take notes, and the two would piece it together, until the words were Tamang's own.

At her exhibition's recent opening night, Tamang was surprised by the size of the crowd.

In a particularly touching tribute, two of her friends came dressed as giant pink poodles, a nod to the poodles that recur in her work. Her friend Dimity Shepherd sang. Lipstick entrepreneur Poppy King turned up.

It's a following both Luttin and Tamang hope the show will help grow, as Tamang makes the leap to a professional career.

For Tamang, though, it comes back to the work.

"It's what keeps me going," she says. "I love bringing people happiness, and connecting."

title: Low pay, poor conditions drive apprenticeship dropouts
text:
About half of Australia's apprentices drop out early, and experts say workplace conditions, low pay, and a lack of support are among the reasons.

National Centre for Vocational Education Research figures show 52 per cent of apprentices and trainees who started in 2020 did not complete their training within the expected four years.

Its latest figures show the number of apprenticeship and traineeship contracts in progress fell 8.6 per cent in the year to December 2025, including a 17.1 per cent fall in non-trade contracts.

Among those who left before completing, about 85 per cent said something could have helped them finish, with changes to their job or workplace the most common response.

Kira Clarke says students need exposure to a wide range of careers to avoid possible disappointment. (Supplied: Brotherhood of St Laurence)

Kira Clarke, who leads employment, education and training policy at the Brotherhood of St Laurence, said a range of financial and workplace pressures make it difficult for apprentices to complete their training.

"There's a number of reasons for this, low wages, inflexible delivery timelines and rigid structures, and also inconsistent readiness of employers to support and mentor apprentices," Ms Clarke said.

She also said many apprentices had a limited understanding of the jobs and training pathways available to them before beginning their apprenticeship.

"For a lot of young people, the visibility they have to the types of jobs they might be interested in is often quite limited to what jobs their family do, what their teachers have told them about what their immediate circle of friends and community are doing," Ms Clarke said.

" There's a lot of anxiety about, 'Am I making the right choice for the type of job that I think I'll enjoy?' "

Personal experiences matter

Federation University emeritus professor Erica Smith said that even after young people choose an apprenticeship, their experience at work often determines whether they finish.

Erica Smith says better data is needed to understand why apprentices aren't completing their apprenticeships. (Supplied: Erica Smith)

"When you look at the data on why people don't complete, they say it's to do with the job, not to do with the training," Professor Smith said.

"An apprenticeship is a job, and people leave jobs."

Professor Smith said the figures gave only broad reasons for why apprentices left and did not show what they experienced at work each day or what ultimately pushed them to quit.

"I've recommended much better data be collected from apprentices to find out: are they happy, why are they happy, why aren't they happy, what's bothering them?" she said.

Professor Smith said efforts to improve completion rates needed to look beyond workforce demand and recognise the person undertaking the apprenticeship.

"There's actually a person there," she said.

"Let's think about apprenticeships as being for people."

Earn and learn

With experts pointing to low pay, poor workplace support and limited regional options as reasons apprentices leave, Federation University is looking at models that aim to better combine study with paid work.

Pro vice-chancellor of VET and pathways Darren Gray said students could earn an income while completing their qualification and gaining workplace experience.

Federation University is looking at what could help prevent apprenticeship dropouts. (Supplied: Federation University)

"As the cost-of-living increases, this is even more important for many students," Mr Gray said.

"This is particularly important in regional communities, where vocational pathways are critical to meeting workforce demand across both trade and non-trade industries."

He said some "earn-and-learn" models meant students have access to wellbeing services, literacy and numeracy support, scholarships, free food and other help.

"This support can make a life-changing difference for students who may be balancing work, family and study commitments," Mr Gray said.

He said that for apprentices facing those competing pressures, that extra support could make the difference between leaving early and completing their qualification.

Embattled western Sydney housing developer Bathla Group has collapsed into voluntary administration, leaving hundreds of buyers who purchased off-the-plan homes in limbo. Documents filed with the corporate regulator on Tuesday morning reveal Teneo has been appointed as administrator of the company, and its hundreds of related entities including Universal Property Group and Raj & Jai Construction. Bathla Group has collapsed. Louie Douvis In an Instagram post on the company’s page, founder and director Bhart Bhushan described the voluntary administration as the “orderly restructure of business” and blamed the decision on “a perfect storm” of declining sales, rising construction costs and the federal government’s May budget. “Our first thoughts are with our employees and the customers who have put their faith in us to deliver their dream of home ownership,” he said. “It is my sincere hope this process can allow that to happen by working collaboratively with the administrators, our suppliers, contractors and lending partners.”

In a statement, Bathla chief executive Robert Loader said the company recognised it was a “difficult situation” and said the appointment of administrators was “in the best interest of all stakeholders”. “The business has been through a period of declining sales and falling property prices, while construction costs have increased,” he said. “We will work constructively with the administrators to support the continued delivery of much-needed housing for western Sydney.” The collapse has left buyers who purchased off the plan unsure about what to do. Last week the Herald reported that buyers who had purchased apartments off the plan at Bathla’s Kembla Grange development had been unable to move in after the completion date for the project, which was originally slated for December 2025, had been extended four times. Janice Cahill, who bought an apartment at the development, said the delays have “really and truly” affected her mental health. When Marie Sinclair, whose elderly parents bought an apartment in the same building, visited the site in September last year, she found doors with keys left unattended, graffitied walls, half-finished copper piping and multiple broken surfaces.

Advertisement

On Tuesday morning she called her real estate agent, asking what the collapse meant, and was assured the project was continuing. Building Commission NSW, the state’s construction watchdog, has undertaken more than 40 inspections of Bathla sites over the past few months. It identified defects at the Kembla Grange development. When asked why the completion date for the project had been pushed back, the spokesperson for Bathla said it was “due to unforeseen site delays with some external works … Completion is forecast for November”. Janice Cahill is hoping to move in to her new home later this year. Wolter Peeters On Friday, Building Commission NSW confirmed it had issued penalties and imposed extensive licence conditions on Raj & Jai Construction and its director, after finding they engaged in improper conduct.

Advertisement

It found the company had carried out work at two properties in Schofields without the mandatory Home Building Compensation Fund (HBCF) insurance being in place, and that its director, on behalf of Raj & Jai Construction, made misleading statements in the applications for the two HBCF insurance certificates. When the HBCF documentation for these properties was submitted in 2024, work had almost been completed, but the applications for the certificates stated that work was just beginning. Raj & Jai Construction was fined $45,000, and its director, $9000. “I accept that that’s not [a huge penalty] but these penalties were for these two particular offences and they were proportionate to those offences,” Building Commissioner James Sherrard told budget estimates on Monday. Sherrard had previously said: “During disciplinary proceedings we found Raj & Jai Construction did not have the governance or compliance systems in place we expect of a large builder in NSW.”

title: Records tumble and so do robots at China’s humanoid Olympics
text:
Advertisement

Analysis WorldAsiaChina relations Records tumble and so do robots at China’s humanoid Olympics Lisa Visentin August 25, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beijing: At the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, the machines proved they are becoming faster, higher, and stronger, even as their practical utility beyond the athletics track remains uncertain. This is the second time China has hosted the games – an unofficial robot Olympics of its own making – which is designed to showcase its national talent against a backdrop of intensifying geopolitical rivalry in the high-tech sphere. Loading With the 100 metres sprint final still to go, the hot ticket is Chinese robot Tiangong Ultra. It took down Usain Bolt’s record in the heats on Saturday, clocking a 9.39-second dash and shaving 0.19 seconds off the Jamaican superstar’s time, which remains unbeaten by humans since 2009. The Tiangong team struck again on Sunday, claiming victory in the 400 metres final for both the small and large humanoid categories, the latter smashing a 2016 Olympic world record in the process.

Advertisement

If the competitors’ blank faces could express human emotion, they would surely depict sheer terror. The robots fanged it around the track with the unhinged gait of someone fleeing an axe murderer – staggering head forward, arms slicing wildly, on the cusp of falling with each step. Curious spectators have flocked to the National Speed Skating Oval, repurposed from the 2022 Winter Olympics, to watch the spectacle of humanoids competing across events including soccer, martial arts, tennis and athletics. This year’s competition added other scenario-based tests designed to demonstrate dexterity, such as block building, food preparation and storage packing. A humanoid robot falls to the ground before the competition starts the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing. Fairfax Media Robot teams face off in a soccer match. Fairfax Media Naturally, the games function as a giant marketing campaign for Chinese companies eager to attract the eyes (and wallets) of investors in what is a viciously competitive domestic sector already oversaturated with players. The future is clouded by strategic rivalry after the US banned the import of next-generation Chinese humanoids in a bid to protect its own nascent industry.

Advertisement

The events are less about the robots’ achievements on the day and more about signalling their future capabilities and commercial potential, which remain unclear for now. “I heard a robot ran faster than Bolt – that blew my mind,” says Li Ran, a 23-year-old university student who was watching the events with a friend. “If they get even more advanced and something bad happens, humans could be in serious danger.” For now, experts generally agree that humanoids are a long way from being autonomously deployed to carry out complex tasks in real-world environments. A humanoid robot developed by Galbot plays tennis against Chinese tennis star Zheng Jie at the games. Fairfax Media

Advertisement

We can – and maybe, in the name of scientific endeavour alone, we should – applaud man’s ingenuity in developing a lookalike machine that can now outrun man himself. Related Article China relations China is dominating the EV market. Now it wants to do the same with robots But when it comes to closing the capability gap between man and robot, perhaps the humanoids’ greatest achievement to date is their ability to reflect a collective exasperation with the human condition, with a distinctly 21st-century panache. Is there a more apt metaphor for existential futility than a humanoid sprinting at top speed in pursuit of man-made glory, only to fail to brake in time and slam into a safety barrier? And from there, stumble backwards, plough headfirst into the ground, and break at the waist, sending sparks shooting into the sky?

Advertisement

The Greeks had Sisyphus and his boulder. We have humanoids doomed to careen into walls on command. In a feat that launched a thousand memes, one robot did exactly this in the training heats before the games kicked off, giving the event’s promoters (the Chinese government) the hype and virality they were looking for. The competition has been joyously rich with crashes, face-plants, false starts and blowouts, the best ones sending limbs flying and requiring extinguishers for spot fires. Fallen comrades were carted off the tracks on blue stretchers. All of which makes the robot games a hoot, while injecting a degree of freewheeling chaos into Beijing’s image, otherwise better known for its staid and stage-managed public spectacles.

Advertisement

The concept of “world”, however, functions the same as it does in Major League Baseball’s World Series – a name suggestive of a greater level of international buy-in than it has. About 95 per cent of the 666 competing teams are Chinese, a share that mirrors China’s dominance in the global humanoid robotics sector. Despite their speed, the robots still lack the dexterity and finesse of their controllers. There will be no bidding war for the broadcast rights for humanoid soccer any time soon, unless there is a sudden explosion in demand for painfully slow midfield play, clunky defending, and goals that dribble over the line. Don’t take it from me. The kids of China’s Generation Alpha, the first digital natives to grow up in robotised megacities, are a little underwhelmed.

Advertisement

“Their reaction ability isn’t strong enough, so they miss chances. In terms of soccer performance, there’s still room for improvement,” says 12-year-old Zha Wenqi, who was watching with his dad. The Australian sharemarket advanced in early trade, boosted by energy stocks after a strong result from local oil giant Woodside Energy, shrugging off a mixed finish on Wall Street. The S&P/ASX 200 was up 37.9 points, or 0.4 per cent, at 9141 just before 11am AEST, with all 11 industry sectors bar real estate in the green. The local market added 0.5 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.47¢. Reporting season continues, with Coles and Woodside Energy among companies that released results this morning. The Reserve Bank will publish minutes of its latest meeting, when it kept interest rates on hold, later this morning. Wall Street drifted to a mixed finish, providing little direction for the ASX. Bloomberg Woodside gained 2.2 per cent after saying a 44 per cent jump in the average selling price for its oil pushed its operating revenue up 28 per cent from a year ago to $US4.19 billion ($5.9 billion) in the June quarter, even as its production output was hit by maintenance work at its Pluto Train 1 LNG processing plant in WA and recovery from cyclone impacts. The sales bump lifted its net profit for the six months to June 30 by 7 per cent to $US1.33 billion.

Bulls N’ Bears Big Hits looks at notable drill intercepts reported last week to the ASX. Bulls N’ Bears Big Hits looks at notable drill hits recently reported to the ASX last week, led by Sun Silver, Manhattan Gold Corporation and QMines Ltd. So let’s dive in. SUN SILVER (ASX: SS1) Project: Maverick Springs project, Nevada, United States Hit: 98.3 metres grading 120.3 grams per tonne silver equivalent from 173 metres

Advertisement

Sun Silver took out last week’s top spot after delivering a monster silver-equivalent intercept from its Maverick Springs project in Nevada, with drilling extending mineralisation beyond the boundaries of the current resource estimate and further strengthening the project’s growth credentials. The headline result of 98.3m at 120.3g/t silver equivalent from 173m depth included a substantial higher-grade core running 47.6m at 200.6g/t silver equivalent. The main result combined 65.7g/t silver and 0.67g/t gold across the broader interval, with the higher-grade zone carrying 119.6g/t silver and 1.05g/t gold from 176.8m. The width and grade combination immediately placed the hole among the most notable precious metal intercepts reported to the ASX during the week. Importantly, the hole was drilled beyond the limits of the current mineral resource estimate, meaning the intercept is not merely confirming known mineralisation; it could also open the door to future resource growth. That distinction is particularly important in mature projects where investors are increasingly looking for additional ounces rather than simple resource conversion. Wide intercepts are invariably more attractive than narrow high-grade hits because they can deliver more tonnes per vertical metre, provide greater mining flexibility and potentially lower operating costs. In this case, Sun Silver has delivered both width and grade, a combination that is not always easy to find.

Advertisement

The higher-grade core within the broader mineralised envelope is also encouraging, as it may support improved project economics in future development studies. Investors and mining engineers alike tend to focus on these richer zones because they often form the basis of early mine schedules and stronger cash flows. Nevada remains one of the world’s premier mining jurisdictions and hosts numerous large silver and gold operations. Maverick Springs already features the scale necessary to attract market attention, but results like this suggest the project still has considerable room for expansion. The company’s latest drilling suggests mineralisation remains open within the current target area and demonstrates the consistency of the Maverick Springs system. As further drilling continues to push beyond known boundaries, Sun Silver appears well-positioned to build on an already substantial resource base. For sheer scale, grade and resource-growth potential, Sun Silver’s Nevada result is the clear standout drill hit of the week. MANHATTAN GOLD (ASX: MHC)

Advertisement

Project: Jaws prospect, Hook Lake project, Nunavut, Canada Hit: 41.15 metres grading 4.66 grams per tonne gold from 83.82 metres Few things excite the market more than an outstanding maiden drilling result and Manhattan Gold delivered exactly that this week with a spectacular intercept from its Jaws prospect within the company’s Hook Lake project in Nunavut, Canada. The standout hole returned 41.15m at 4.66g/t gold from 83.82m depth, including an exceptional 7.62m zone running 18.67g/t gold and even more eye-catching individual sample intervals included 1.52m assaying 41g/t gold from 89.92m depth and 1.52m going 33.40g/t gold from 86.87m, highlighting the presence of very rich mineralisation within the broader zone. The top intercept was reported from the first batch of assays received from Manhattan’s maiden reverse-circulation drilling program, immediately exceeding expectations. Management noted that the result was both wider and higher grade than nearby historical drilling, suggesting that previous exploration may have significantly underestimated the scale and quality of the mineralised system.

Advertisement

One of the more interesting aspects of the announcement was the company’s revised geological interpretation arising from its improved spatial control across the Jaws system. More recent drilling has indicated the principal mineralised structure sits some 20m to 30m northwest of where historical records suggested it was located. That shift may sound minor, but in exploration terms it can be the difference between intersecting the edge of a system and drilling directly through its most prospective zones. The current interpretation is that the new hole may have intersected one of a series of high-grade shoots within a much larger gold-mineralised corridor. Such shoots often form the backbone of successful underground and open-pit gold operations and become priority targets for follow-up drilling campaigns. The Jaws prospect already hosts a substantial historical, non-JORC compliant 1980’s resource estimate of 3.4Mt at 2.38g/t gold for 285,000 ounces of gold, but the latest drilling points to significant potential upside beyond what has previously been recognised. Adding to the excitement, the hole also finished in mineralisation, intersecting another gold-bearing zone near the bottom of the drill hole, suggesting the system may continue at depth, but for now it remains incompletely tested.

Advertisement

With additional assay results still pending from the broader drilling program, Manhattan Gold now finds itself in the enviable position of having delivered an outstanding discovery-style intercept while still retaining considerable near-term news flow. For a maiden campaign, it is hard to ask for much more than a shallow, wide, high-grade gold intersection backed by a compelling exploration narrative. This result firmly establishes Jaws as one of the more intriguing gold stories to emerge this week. QMines’ Rig 19 drilling from a barge in the flooded open pit at the Mt Chalmers project in Queensland. Drilling is also being undertaken around the open pit margins. QMINES (ASX: QML) Project: Mt Chalmers project, Queensland

Advertisement

Hit: 35 metres grading 2.88 per cent copper, 0.75 grams per tonne gold and 3.3 grams per tonne silver from 107 metres. Rounding out this week’s Big Hits podium is QMines, which delivered a powerful copper-gold intercept from its Mt Chalmers project, 25 kilometres northeast of Rockhampton in Queensland, reinforcing the project’s credentials as one of Australia’s more significant emerging base-metal opportunities. The company’s headline result returned 35m grading 2.88 per cent copper, 0.75g/t gold and 3.3g/t silver from a depth of 107m. Within the broader zone, an even higher-grade core delivered 31m at 3.22 per cent copper and 0.83g/t gold from 110m. A second hole delivered 16m assaying 1.17 per cent copper and 1.58g/t gold from 66m, which included 2m going 4.22 per cent copper and 5.38g/t gold. A further broad zone in the same hole returned 21m at 0.84 per cent copper and 0.83g/t gold from 89m, including 5m at 1.52 per cent copper and 1.09g/t gold.

Advertisement

The drilling also produced exceptional individual samples grading up to 10.45 per cent copper and 7.02g/t gold in the first hole, while the second hole gave up 5.12 per cent copper and 9.52g/t gold, numbers guaranteed to attract attention in any exploration program. As with Sun Silver, what makes the results particularly impressive is the combination of width and grade. QMines has also reported both, pointing to a robust mineralised system capable of supporting further resource growth. The accompanying gold values provide an additional bonus, as the occasionally hefty precious-metal credits offer the potential to improve project economics materially. The intercepts also include silver and zinc, highlighting the polymetallic nature of the Mt Chalmers system and demonstrating the persistence and continuity of mineralisation within the target area. The strong copper grades over substantial widths increase confidence in the project’s development potential, particularly when ongoing drilling continues to confirm the geological model. Copper remains one of the most sought-after commodities globally as demand from electrification, renewable energy generation, electric vehicles and power transmission infrastructure continues to grow. As a result, high-quality copper discoveries and expansions continue to attract considerable market attention.

Advertisement

The latest result strengthens QMines’ position within Australia’s copper exploration sector and suggests further upside remains available as drilling advances across the broader project. The current Mt Chalmers estimated resource stands at a combined inferred, indicated and measured 11.3 million tonnes averaging 0.75 per cent copper, 0.42g/t gold, 0.23 per cent zinc and 4/6g/t silver, of which 88.5 per cent is in the two higher resource categories. The company also has a combined total of 10.5 million tonnes in three other resources at Woods Shaft, near Mt Chalmers and at Develin Creek and Mt Mackenzie, 100km and 150km northwest of Rockhampton, respectively. QMines has maintained continuous drilling at Mt Chalmers since March and has so far completed 24 holes for 2890m, including 18 diamond and RC pre-collar holes for 2351m across the deposit. More than 1200 samples have been submitted to ALS, providing a strong pipeline of upcoming assay results. The company says it expects further significant news, with assays still awaited from another seven drill holes amid its ongoing 10,000m multi-rig drilling campaign.

While precious-metals stories may have dominated headlines this week, QMines’ thick, latest high-grade copper-gold intercepts ensure it has earned its place among this week’s most significant drill results. title: Trump's visa crackdown plan could affect thousands seeking asylum in the US
text:
In brief The US government is set to revoke business and tourism visas for foreigners seeking asylum.

If enacted, it would be the largest mass revocation of visas in US history.

The Trump administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum status in the United States.

If it happens, the move would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history and would likely face legal challenges.

Unless challenged or revised, the US state department is expected to announce in the coming weeks the revocation of so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum, according to state department documents obtained by the Associated Press (AP) and two US officials. The action will be taken in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

"We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently," state department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said.

He declined to comment on the number of visas that might be revoked, saying "as the process will be ongoing, the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis".

The revocations would not necessarily result in their immediate deportation, the officials said. Most of those with asylum cases currently pending would be recategorised but would lose their status as business or tourism travellers, according to the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the revocations are not final yet.

Since US President Donald Trump took office for his second term last year, his administration has steadily ramped up restrictions on visa applicants — demanding more information about their social media histories, requiring the posting of expensive bonds to process visas, and outright banning the issuance of visas to citizens of certain countries.

In a social media post on Tuesday, US deputy secretary of state Christopher Landau called out people who he said try to use tourist and business visas to get into the US and then apply for asylum.

"People in the US and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims," Landau said in a post on X. "Asylum isn’t supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law."

Landau cited the case of a Colombian citizen who came to the US in 2015 on a tourist visa and then applied for asylum.

B1 visas are generally issued for business trips and B2 visas are generally issued for tourism, family visits or medical care. It was not immediately clear from the documents or the officials how many of these visa holders are seeking or have sought asylum in the US and would be affected by the revocations.

Current applicants for B1 and B2 visas are asked to affirm that they will not apply for asylum in the US and prove that they intend to return to their home countries.

In the past 18 months, the state department has revoked about 175,000 visas for people who have been convicted or accused of crimes ranging from drunken driving to rape and robbery, as well as for people who have spoken out publicly against US policies, particularly in the Middle East.

The administration has also moved to crack down on so-called birth tourism, a practice the administration claims is used by foreign pregnant women to come to the US to give birth so that their child will benefit from birthright citizenship.

Trump has tried several times to end birthright citizenship, but those challenges have been rejected by courts, including the US Supreme Court.

The state department documents obtained by AP suggest screening of current B1 and B2 visa holders began after the state department received information about asylum requests from the US Citizenship and Immigration Services.
